title: Solid Friction

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Force That Opposes Every Push

Friction is the contact force opposing relative (or attempted) motion between surfaces. It is indispensable — walking, brakes, nail grips — and costly — worn engines, wasted fuel. The syllabus asks for the laws of solid friction and their experimental verifications, plus incline numericals.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Static friction** | Opposes the *start* of motion; self-adjusting up to a maximum |
| **Limiting friction** | Maximum static friction just before sliding begins: $f_s^{max} = \mu_s N$ |
| **Kinetic friction** | Opposes motion once sliding: $f_k = \mu_k N$, roughly constant and slightly less than limiting friction |
| **Normal reaction** | The surface's perpendicular push: $N = mg$ on level ground, $mg\cos\theta$ on an incline |
| **Coefficient of friction (μ)** | Ratio of friction to normal reaction — dimensionless, typically 0.05–1.5 |

### 2.1 Laws of solid friction

1. Friction acts **opposite to the direction of attempted/actual relative motion**, along the surfaces in contact.
2. Friction is **proportional to the normal reaction**: $f \propto N$.
3. Friction is **independent of the apparent area of contact** (for a given normal reaction).
4. Kinetic friction is **independent of the relative velocity** (at ordinary speeds).
5. Kinetic friction is slightly **less than limiting static friction**.

### 2.2 Experimental verifications

- **Proportional to N:** a block on a table is pulled by a spring balance at constant speed; repeat with weights stacked on the block — the reading scales with total weight; a graph of f against N is a straight line whose slope is μ.
- **Independent of area:** repeat with the block on different faces (different contact areas) — the balance reading is unchanged.
- **Independent of speed:** pull at different steady speeds — the reading stays (approximately) constant.
- **Angle of repose:** a block on an adjustable incline just slides at angle θ_r; resolving gives $\mu = \tan\theta_r$ — a direct measurement.

### 2.3 Incline relations

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| On the point of sliding down | $\mu_s = \tan\theta_r$ (angle of repose) |
| Sliding down with friction | $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$ |
| Force to pull up the incline at constant speed | $F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)$ |

## 3. Worked Numericals

**Q1 (3m, 2023):** A block of mass 5 kg rests on a horizontal plane. The coefficient of static friction is 0.4. What horizontal force is needed to start the block moving? (g = 10 m/s²)
$N = mg = 50$ N; $f_{limiting} = \mu_s N = 0.4 \times 50 = 20$ N. **A force just over 20 N starts the motion.**

**Q2 (3m, 2021):** A block of mass 10 kg rests on a rough inclined plane of angle 30°. If the coefficient of friction is 0.2, find the frictional force (and the acceleration). (g = 10 m/s²)
$N = mg\cos30° = 100 \times 0.866 = 86.6$ N; $f = \mu N = 0.2 \times 86.6 = 17.3$ N.
Driving component: $mg\sin30° = 50$ N > 17.3 N, so it slides: $a = g(\sin30° - \mu\cos30°) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 3.27$ m/s².
**Friction ≈ 17.3 N up the plane; a ≈ 3.3 m/s² down the plane.**

**Q3 (3m, 2024):** A block just begins to slide down a rough incline when the angle of inclination is 30°. Calculate the coefficient of static friction.
At the point of sliding, gravity's component equals limiting friction: $mg\sin\theta = \mu mg\cos\theta → \mu = \tan\theta = \tan30° = 0.577$. **μ ≈ 0.58.**

## 4. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 13:** friction is a contact force entering Newton's-law applications; the incline formulas combine the second law with friction.
- **To Work/Energy (Unit 5):** friction dissipates mechanical energy as heat — the reason slides stop.
- **To Circular Motion:** friction supplies the centripetal force for cornering vehicles (banking topic).
- **To real life:** tyres, brakes, belts and nails need friction; engines and skates fight it with lubrication (replacing solid with fluid friction).

### 5.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Using $N = mg$ on an incline — there $N = mg\cos\theta$.
2. Forgetting that static friction **self-adjusts** — it equals the applied force up to its limit, not always μN.
3. Saying friction depends on contact area — the law says it does not.
4. Confusing the angle of repose relation ($\mu = \tan\theta_r$) with $\sin$ or $\cos$.
5. Mixing μ_s and μ_k in one problem without saying which.

notes: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

**Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

**Angle of friction (λ):** the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant reaction (normal + friction) when slipping is about to occur. tan λ = μ_s. The resultant reaction makes angle λ with the normal.

**Angle of repose (θ_r):** the steepest angle of a slope at which a body just remains at rest. At this angle, mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r → tan θ_r = μ_s. So θ_r = λ — the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

**Worked example — body on a slope:** a 10 kg block on a 25° slope (μ_s = 0.5). Does it slide? tan 25° = 0.466 < 0.5 → no, it stays. Static friction = mg sin 25° = 41.5 N (less than μ_sN = 0.5 × 92.4 = 46.2 N).

**Worked example — pulling a block:** a 5 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3). Pulled by a 20 N force at 30° above horizontal. Normal N = mg − F sin 30° = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Friction = 0.3 × 39 = 11.7 N. Net force = 20 cos 30° − 11.7 = 5.6 N. a = 5.6/5 = 1.12 m/s².

**NEB exam focus:** distinguish static vs kinetic friction; solve slope problems (does it slide? find acceleration); angle of repose and its equality with angle of friction; pulling/pushing at an angle (changes the normal, hence friction).
confusion: ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

❌ 'Friction depends on the area of contact.' ✅ For a given normal force, friction is (approximately) independent of area. A wide tyre and a narrow tyre with the same load have the same maximum friction (in the simple model).
❌ 'Static friction is always μ_sN.' ✅ Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN. Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.
❌ 'μ_k > μ_s because sliding is faster.' ✅ μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding. This is why a heavy box jerks when you first push it.
❌ 'The angle of repose depends on the mass of the body.' ✅ tan θ_r = μ_s — mass cancels out. All bodies with the same μ_s have the same angle of repose.

❌ 'Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction because the force is smaller.' ✅ Pulling upward reduces the normal (N = mg − F sin θ), which reduces friction. Pushing downward increases the normal and friction.

specificConditions: **Static vs. Kinetic Threshold:** The maximum static friction $f_s^{\max} = \mu_s N$ is the *upper bound* for static friction. Static friction is a *variable* force that matches the applied force up to this limit. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ applies *only* when sliding occurs, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.

**Normal Force Dependency:** Friction is proportional to the *normal reaction*, not the weight. Any vertical force component (pulling up, pushing down, incline) changes $N$, which directly changes the friction force. Always compute $N$ first.

**Area Independence (Ideal Model):** The laws of friction assume friction is independent of the apparent contact area (Coulomb's model). This holds well for dry, rigid surfaces but breaks down for soft materials, lubricated contacts, or adhesive forces where real contact area matters.

summary: Friction opposes attempted or actual relative motion along surfaces. **Static friction self-adjusts** up to the limiting value μ_sN; kinetic friction runs at μ_kN, slightly smaller and nearly speed-independent. The laws: friction opposes relative motion, is proportional to normal reaction, and ignores contact area — verified by spring-balance pulls with added weights (straight-line f–N graph), face-swaps (same reading) and the **angle of repose**, where μ = tan θ_r. Incline numericals flow from $N = mg\cos\theta$: a 5 kg block with μ_s = 0.4 needs just over 20 N to start (NEB 2023); a 10 kg block on 30° with μ = 0.2 feels 17.3 N of friction and slides at 3.3 m/s² (NEB 2021); a block just sliding at 30° fixes μ = tan 30° ≈ 0.58 (NEB 2024).

subtopics.name: Types
points: Static friction acts before motion starts
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction

subtopics.name: The laws
points: Friction is proportional to the normal reaction: f = mu N
Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact
Static friction exceeds kinetic friction for the same surfaces

subtopics.name: Angle of friction
points: tan(lambda) = mu, where lambda is the angle of friction
The resultant of normal reaction and limiting friction makes this angle with the normal
Angle of repose equals the angle of friction

subtopics.name: Angle of repose
points: The steepest angle at which a body rests without sliding
Independent of the mass of the body

subtopics.name: Microscopic origin
points: Friction arises from adhesion at real contact points and surface roughness
Real contact area is far smaller than apparent area, which is why area does not matter
Lubrication works by separating surfaces with a fluid film

subtopics.name: Necessary friction
points: Walking, braking, belt drives and nails all depend on friction
Friction is not simply a nuisance to be eliminated
Anti-lock brakes exploit static friction by preventing skidding
